projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Charles Olson was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Charles W. Olson, also known as Bill. Mr. Olson served with the U.S. Army Air Force. He served in Panama, India, and China, and his highest rank was 1st Lieutenant. I'm Tom Swope. We recorded this at Mr. Olson's office at Euclid, Ohio, on March 1, 2002. Bill's age at the time of this recording was 78. Where were you living when the war started?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: When the war started, I was living in Cleveland Heights, and I was a freshman at Case, taking engineering out at Case, and used to ride the streetcar down, which is no longer available. I'd grown up; I'd graduated from Heights High School in 1941, so, see, the timing was right there. I remember on December 7th we had a fraternity pledge play on that Sunday afternoon, and when we all got down there, of course the radio announcement was there and we'd heard of the bombing and the guys were marching around saying, "I'm in the Army now." I thought I was -- I thought I was going to be deferred to graduate, see, 'cause I was 18. This goes into the fall of '42. I was a sophomore then, and the Air Force and the Navy offered deferment for engineering students. And as you read in my history, I signed up for that. And interesting, there was only six of us out of all of those that took the test that passed. And the interesting thing was -- color-blind, so many of the guys, they didn't know that. So that was in November of '42, and I was supposed to get deferred for three years.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were drafted in '43. Well, why didn't you end up in the infantry?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: No, I was not drafted. See, I volunteered for the Reserve --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: -- in order to get the deferment --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: -- and they called the Reserves.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Called up the Reserves. Were you in the Army Air Corps Reserves or just the Army?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: What did they call it? I think they called it -- I don't remember what they did call it. It was a deferment, and there was a lot of paperwork to it. I don't really remember what that was all about.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So the intent was to let you finish school and then serve.

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Yes. Because in those days there weren't an awful lot of college kids. Engineering schools are pretty -- generally, compared to today, they were very tiny. In my class at Case there was six of us. They took metallurgy, that finally graduated. Now, you know, there's 60 or 100, and that's a small department. So I went into San Antonio, Texas, and there we had to take a whole bunch of tests for classification, whether you're going to be a pilot, navigator, or bombardier. Then there was -- I don't know how exactly they separated them, but I qualified for all three of them. So I got to choose, and I chose pilot. I was in San -- I was lucky. I was in San Antonio classification center, I think, only a couple of weeks, and then I went across the street to preflight school, which was really in the Army. See, I'd only been in the Army for -- in uniform for two or three weeks. Now I started marching and doing callisthenics, running all over the place, and it was -- it was, in a way, fun. Looking back, it was fun. But at the time, we were going crazy trying to keep up with what was going on, besides all the marching and callisthenics, we had -- we were taking classes, preflight classes in navigation and aviation and all kinds of things like that, and we stayed there for nine weeks. Do you want me to go?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure, yeah, keep going. Yeah, that's fine. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: We stayed there for nine weeks, four and a half weeks underclassmen and four and a half weeks upperclassmen, and then I went to Sikeston, Missouri, for primary flying school, and I'd never been in an airplane in my life! It was quite an experience. Sikeston was a private flying school in those days. See, keep in mind, this is not military, period. There was nothing before that. The Air Force in the '30S was Randolph Field in Texas. But I don't know how they could put it all together, because it really was put together. And I think in our class at Sikeston there was probably 80 -- 60, 80 cadets, aviation cadets, and there we went to school half a day and flew half a day in a PT-19, which is a low-wing, 60-horsepower monoplane. It was very easy to fly. Let's see, I think after -- after something like ten hours, we had to solo the PT-19. Well, a lot of guys flunked out. A lot of guys didn't make it. And I was very happy that I did [laughter].

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything specifically about that first solo flight?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: No, not really. The first solo, I don't really remember. I remember my instructor's name was Swanson, and they'd say over the loudspeaker, "Okay, Olson with Mr. Swanson, you're next." [Laughter.]

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Nervous?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I'll never forget the first time we turned that airplane upside down. He said -- he did it, I didn't. He said, Okay, now just -- put your arms in the side of the cockpit. It was an open cockpit. We're going to go upside down. We did, and really, I was held in by my seat belt. I half fell out of the airplane [laughter]. My hand was rubbing it. But Mr. Swanson was a good guy, and we got along fine. After -- after the first solo flight, we did just flying. We'd -- by yourself, no formations or anything like that, and we'd take off and fly for an hour, do various things, the loops and rolls and chandelles, which nobody knows what it is anymore. The primary flying school was sort of easy. We got -- it was pretty much away from the military. There was very little marching. We had callisthenics, of course. We went to school half a day for three or four hours, and there we studied all kinds more of navigation, and I don't -- I don't think we had a link trainer at primary. But after 9 weeks there -- 4 1/2 weeks underclassman, 4 1/2 weeks upperclassman -- I went to Independence -- yeah, Independence, Kansas, for basic flying training, and there we got into a -- certified on the BT, BT-19, I think it was, low-wing, all-craft Vultee airplane. It was a terrible airplane. Nobody liked it. It was underpowered and -- but it was a step up from the old 70-horsepower PT-19s. It was a BT-13 is what it was, not a BT-19. So we got the BT-13s, but the basic was, yeah, was back in the Army, all we had was marching and drilling and callisthenics and rigid, stand-up-and-salute stuff that we hadn't had. And keep in mind, I've been in the Army now for what, ten weeks. They tried to make soldiers out of us. Well, nine weeks of basic in the BT-13 was pretty much a continuation, just gradually moving up. There we started a little bit of formation flying. We had, of course, we had an instructor and we had to wait awhile, X number of hours before we could solo, but by that time, most of us were pilots. We were able to fly. You know, I mean, we'd been through primary and had 70 or 80 hours, I think. And then the basic -- well, time went very fast. I don't remember all the details. I don't think we got any days off. I think we were in there seven days a week and flying and going to school. And then we went to advanced flying school, which is Eagle Pass, Texas. And I talked to a guy here, oh, a couple of years ago from Texas, and I says, I said, "Do you ever get to Eagle Pass?" And he said, "Oh, yeah." I said, "I used to fly down there." He said, "Did you really?" He said, "Well, they've torn up that runway. It's now a housing project." [Laughter]. But advanced line school was great -- greatly relaxed from basic. Sure, we were still in the Army, we were still saluting and still acting military, but the intensity was on how to fly, how to make that airplane do what you want. Then we had an AT-6 North American, one of the best planes, I think, that I ever flew, 450-horsepower. It had low wing, it'd go. It would go. In a dive, you could get up to 3, 400 miles an hour. And there we did a lot of formation flying, a lot of acrobatics. We went down to a place called Matagorda Island, which is in the Gulf of Mexico, for gunnery training. We had 2, I think 2, 3-men -- or 3-millimeter guns that were in the nose of the plane, and they shot between the propeller. They were timed so that the bullets would get out between the propeller blades. We had flights of four guys. And it was fun. We were having fun. And they had -- they towed a target, and I'm not sure, the target was -- I think it was 3 feet high and about 20 feet long, and it was a screen, a white screen. Well, we'd have these bullets, we've got 100 rounds in each gun. They dipped the tip of the bullet in a color paint for each pilot, different color, okay, so when it goes through that white screen, it leaves a mark, and you can count how many you hit. Well, here we thought we were hot pilots in our airplane. They came -- it was towed by a tow ship and we -- we'd come flying in and shoot the bullets and you'd have traces and you can see where they're going. And the first time they dropped that target, we could hardly wait to see it. There wasn't a hole in it [laughter]. 800 shots, and not a hole in the target. We missed 100%. Well, that definitely improved. I mean, it was -- it was good training. We also had ground gunnery where they had ground targets, big -- they must have been eight feet square with bull's-eyes in them. And we'd come diving in on those, and that was much easier. You could hit that. That was easier. But flying -- and I often thought during the war, I wonder how many of those guys in France and England were really hitting anybody, because I think they qualified to be an expert gunner, I'm not positive, but I think it was 5%, 5% hits. So that went on, that was two weeks. That was a lot of fun. We enjoyed that. And by now we're fairly experienced pilots. I mean, we're flying. We were comfortable in the airplane, and it was a good plane. Then we came back to Eagle Pass for the last, I don't know, two or three weeks. And that's when we checked out in fighter planes, and they had the old P-40 down there. They had a dozen of them or so. And we'd solo, and boy, I remember that first solo flight in the P-40, you're all by yourself, there's nobody to help you, you're doing it all, and you give it the gun and a full throttle, to get up to takeoff speed, and the torque on that engine makes it want to turn off the runway, really. And I remember, I weighed 120 pounds, standing on that rotor to keep it going straight down the runway [laughter]. And I took -- finally got the thing off the ground. Well, it wasn't too long because they go pretty quick. And I flew straight and level, I bet, for 20 miles before I was ready to turn it. [laughter]. It was really sort of fun. But we got accustomed to that -- to the feel of it, to the P-40. And I went -- there was, I don't know, I think we probably flew it maybe 20 hours, something like that. But in addition we were still flying the AT-6s. We were still having formation practice with the AT-6, and we had cross-country. And in those days they had -- dit dot quarters in -- in the circle of radio signals, they had in quadrants, and we -- I remember we went one flight, my first airplane was grounded, so I had to wait for one of the guys to come back with another airplane, and I took off about midnight and we -- I went from Eagle Pass to San Antonio. That was about an hour, as I recall. And then I turned west to the Rio Grande and then turned back south to get -- there was a big triangle. Well, in order to make sure you were on the beam, you had to listen to the radio, dit dot or dot dit, you know, so you'd know which side of the beam you're on. Boy, that is so faint. Really, it was awfully difficult to listen and hear that. Once you get going down the beam, you sort of make "S" curves all the way down the beam. And I remember I got up the next morning, and the bunk on my left and right were both empty. Delbert O'Leary, Olson, O'Leary, Ott --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Delbert O'Leary had landed his plane up at another base, and they found Harry Ott down in the mountains in Mexico. I mean, this is training.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Simple cross-country. It's like, you know, going from here to Ashtabula.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: And so we finally graduated. And I think I got three days, and in those days flying was not -- not available. You know, we were taking trains. And to come from San Antonio, Texas, to Cleveland, it took a day, if you're lucky. I think I was only home for probably less than 24 hours. Then I went back down to San Antonio. Do you want me to keep going?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Went back to San Antonio, and we were assigned our first assignment, and I was assigned to the 6th Air Force at Albrecht Field in Panama. So we took a train -- we had a ball on that train -- from San Antonio to Miami Beach.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kind of things did you do on the train?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Well, we stopped at New Orleans and just had a night of it. And keep in mind, we're -- now we're 19 years old, on our own and 2nd lieutenants with wings. I mean, we thought we were the varies (ph). And we got to Miami Beach, and we stayed at the Floridian Hotel, I remember, which was a stepping point to go. We sat there for two weeks waiting for an airplane. We had nothing to do. All we had to do was report in the morning that we were there, and went to -- went out for breakfast and just had a ball. A lot of fun. Met a bunch of neat gals [laughter]. It was fun. So then we went to -- finally got to Airbrook Field, which was a beautiful permin (ph) air base, headquarters for the 6th Air Force. And by -- the buildings were beautiful, I mean, see, they'd been built in the '30S when they were putting up lawns, and it was just a beautiful place. I remember the officers' club had a great big Mosaic floor with a 6th Air Force emblem laid into it. It was just beautiful. And then -- I don't remember how long we stayed there. Not very long at headquarters. And then we were assigned to a fighter squadron. And I went to the -- what was the number, 56 Fighter Squadron up in Aquadulce, Panama, which was out of the jungle; but it was, I don't know, 80 miles or so from Panama City. And we were all by ourselves. We had a strip, just a strip of cement or blacktop or whatever it was, and a lot of it was just dirt. The taxiways were just dirt. They had the old P-40Cs there, and we took the P-40C -- I don't remember how long I was there. Probably a month or so. Sort of a training squadron. Then I was assigned to a base in -- called Madden Field, which was within two miles of the Panama Canal in the middle of the jungle. We had -- the accommodations were not much. There were no windows, it was all screens. Of course, they didn't need windows. And once again, we had the landings, just the strip carved out of the jungle, and that's when we started flying P-39s. So I flew P-39s. I was in Madden Field for, I don't know, a couple of months. And then I went to -- another field I went to. It was the 51st Fighter Squadron. What's the name of that? It left me. That was another one. But it was near the ocean, near the Pacific Ocean, so the jungle was not quite as thick, but it was still tropics. And we had -- on our parachutes we had these seat packs with the bottom of it -- when you pull out of a dive [laughter], it really hurt. There was -- it was a life raft that was packed in the seat pack, and of course in those days the chute was on the seat. And I was in that field for quite a while. I think I was probably there for four or five months.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is still '43?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: This is '44. Summer of --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Summer of '44. Okay.

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Yeah, spring and summer of '44. That's what those pictures are.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So that rough landing was in Panama?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: No, the rough landing was in India.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. In India.

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: That was in the P-47. So the time in the jungle there, it was pretty good. We -- we were checking on the P-39s and loved them. And we did a lot of formation flying. And our mission was to protect the Canal. And in those days there were nine fighter squadrons on the Canal, and they had alert flights. Each squadron had an alert flight, which was four airplanes that were supposed to get off the ground in five minutes if there was an alert. And they had this radar place called -- I think they called it Quarry, which was right at the mouth of the Canal, and they would search the skies, and if they saw anything, you know, we'd go up and intercept it. Of course, there was never any -- any air attack on Panama, but there were a couple of submarine scares. We went out looking for those guys. And the -- when the Navy came through with an aircraft carrier, they'd attack the Canal, and the Army would defend the Canal. We had a lot of fun doing that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah [laughter].

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Had a lot of fun doing that. I remember one time we had -- this is terrible. We had moved to Howard Field and were flying P-38s and we'd come down for one of these interceptions and the intelligence officer would get all the pilots and ask them questions, you know, how many do you see, blah, blah, blah, blah. Well, there were no two of us agree. So he said, You guys can't even see. So they -- he said, I'd like to go up there one time and I'd be able to count. So I had a P-38, and they took the radio out behind me -- there was no second seat -- and sat Captain Bell on that darn shelf back there with his head sitting right on my shoulder. And we got up and we're doing some pretty quick maneuvering, and he threw up all over me [laughter]. It was awful. And we came back, came back and really gave him the raspberries. Fun experience. When I was in Panama for -- let's see, had to be the fall of '44, yes. And they started shrinking the 6th Air Force. It had nine squadrons. They shrunk it to six. So that's a lot of extra pilots. And the pilots were going back to reassignment all the time. I mean, for a period of two or three months, there were a half a dozen or a dozen a day went back to the States for reassignment. I finally got back to the United States and was reassigned, went to -- first I went to Santa Ana, California, and then -- that sure was awful. Then I went back to -- I drove, my roommate and I, Paul Ensminger -- his picture's there; he was killed -- had a '39 Ford and we drove it from his house in Nebraska to California, then drove it all the way back to Texas. And at Greenville, Texas, I checked out in P-47s. Well, by that time I had 5 or $600 in fighters. And the transfer, checking out was pretty quick. A lot of the guys that came back from Panama went to England and all over, and I was part of six guys that went to India, the China-Burma-India theater. And I remember the trip over there. We -- I think we landed in Bermuda and the Azores, Casablanca, and Tripoli and Cairo and Abadan, Iran, and finally got to Karachi [laughter]. It was -- it took forever. It was one of those old C-54 cargo planes, and I think we were the only guys on board. We landed over there in Karachi and stayed at the British Army base. I don't know what -- what Army it was, but it was a huge base in Karachi. And the British Army had moved back to -- back towards England, just temporary that we were sent there. Then we went -- weren't doing any flying in Karachi. I flew in a B-26 because we were doing some mail carrying. There really wasn't much for us to do, and we were just waiting. And then finally -- finally got assigned to the 89th Fighter Squadron, which was based outside of Calcutta, flying P-47s, of course, and the 89th -- a fighter squadron has 25 pilots and a squadron commander and an adjutant and, I mean, it was a pretty small group, really, over there. Fighter squadrons were not big. They had, you know, like 26 or 27 airplanes, there would be one or two of them on the ground. We were all assigned our own airplane. Our name was on the side of it. That was sort of nice.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Did you put a name on your plane at all?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: No, I don't think I ever did. There was a lot of guys did, but I don't think I ever did. I don't remember doing it. But anyhow, we fussed around Calcutta -- what was the name of that town? Oh, it was awful, 120 degrees and the food was terrible. We used to call it Australian goat [laughter] because they came from Australia. There was no milk. I remember the first breakfast in Karachi the day we landed. We were all sort of hungry. We went into the mess hall and they were serving pancakes, and the darn -- took the butter and the butter wouldn't melt. It was special oleo that -- so it would preserve itself. So, anyhow, we sat around India for around -- I don't know how many months, several months, not doing too much flying because there wasn't much gas. But we flew, you know, three or four hours a week, something like that, just to keep -- keep in training, because we were on our way to China to the China invasion. And early in August of '45, would that be right? '44, when was the A-bomb, '44 or '45?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: '45. The ground crew took the brimmer (ph) road up to Kunming and all that was left was just a handful of pilot -- well, all the pilots were there, and a handful of ground crew. And we were supposed to take off for Kunming in our P-47s on the day that the bomb would have dropped (ph) or a week after, I guess. I don't think that we heard the day that it happened. Communications really weren't that good in those days. But in the meantime I was -- I was flying a lot. We had a B-25 in the squadron and all kinds of military planes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was it easy to adapt to flying a B-26 or a B-25?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Yeah, after P-38s it was. I mean, it was a much easier thing to fly. Call them big trucks. Anyhow, the war was over, and our ground crew was all up in China, and so we sat around, I don't think too long, a couple of weeks, maybe, and then I was assigned to -- I'd only been in India for less than a year, and the guys going home had all been there for more than a year. Some had been there for five or ten years. And they went first. And if you didn't -- weren't there for a year, they reassigned us. And so I was reassigned with several of the guys that came with me to -- up to fly in China, and there we flew C-47s, the cargo planes, the old airline twin-engine or two-engine C-47s.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: [Inaudible].

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: VC-3, and we hauled -- what we were doing was emptying air bases. You know, and when they moved a base out, then we would go haul out whatever they -- the Army thought was worth saving. I remember one time we had a Ping-Pong table [laughter]. It was quite a bit different. The living conditions in China -- see, I'd been in the tropics for two years, and China was like Ohio. It was nice. The weather was decent. It wasn't overwhelming. And the food started to get better. One thing I know we got was fresh eggs, which we had not had in a year. Powdered eggs was the rule in India. And I flew around China for four or five months and we went to Shanghai and all the big cities in China, I landed at. Of course, in those days, being a military visitor, you don't really do too much. You do some looking around, but you always had something to do. And so then I -- after they started clearing out the troops, it finally pretty much concluded what we were doing with the C-47s. We went back to Calcutta and waited for a boat to come home. And one time they were -- there were six brand-new P-47s, and we were going to -- they were going to fly them back to the United States. All contemplating flying a P-47 that far is pretty dull, pretty dull, dry. I mean, you're just sitting flat going straight and level. But at the last minute they decided to junk them, and they bulldozed them together and burned them. It made us sick [laughter].

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Brand-new, huh?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: And then we went -- we finally got in the boat, Eternal Bliss. The Eternal Bliss was a troop ship, and it was big. I remember the officers' quarters -- I guess maybe it was the Air Force officers, we were below waterline, it was crowded, you could hardly roll over in your bed. I mean, just jam-packed. Food was great, because Navy always ate well. And we started off from Calcutta and went around through the Indian Ocean up through the Red Sea and through the -- past the Suez Canal and out the Mediterranean. It was a pretty quiet trip until we got to the Atlantic Ocean. An hour into December we had Thanksgiving dinner out in the Mediterranean, wherever the heck we were, and we thought we were going to get home for Christmas. Well, they got a storm. It was a fantastic storm. The waves were 80 feet tall. That is monstrous. The whole [inaudible] of us who had a newspaper, I still have some at home. It says, "Bliss makes seven knots today." It was just up and down. It would go up and you'd see nothing about sky, and then it'd dive down and you'd see nothing but water. Pretty much everybody but the pilots got seasick. The officers' dining room was empty except for the pilots. It was really a rough sea. And we finally got to New York, and, like, December the 28th, some -- it was after Christmas because we had Christmas dinner on that storm, blew itself out, it leveled so we could get going. And I went to Camp Kilmer, I think was the name of it, in New Jersey, and we spent not long, but it was a rush to get out [laughter]. Went from Camp Kilmer after maybe a day to Indiantown Gap in Pennsylvania. Once again, it was quick. Zip, zip, zip, and you're out. So we got -- missed the train, let's see, the afternoon of December 30th, that would be, and I had to wait until midnight to catch another train to Cleveland that stopped out at the old 55th Street Pennsylvania station. Got into Cleveland December 31st in the morning at 55th Street, had a date with my girl New Year's Eve. That was the end of it. Of course, I was in what they call a terminal leave until March, something like that. And that was pretty much it. The memories still linger. I can still picture things. One thing about the Air Force and pilots was that we were not together a long period. So sure, we have some good friends, but no lifelong friends. You know, there'd be two months, you know, you'd get to know them and like them and have a lot of fun with them, but it's not something in the infantry where you've lived and slept and ate together for six months or a year where you had buddies. The Air Force didn't quite work that way, although there was certainly camaraderie and it was a happy, good group. But the -- we -- I've never had a reunion. I guess there was one. When the heck was that? But once again, the pilots came from all over the country. I mean, you just don't see people that often. The communications and travel was not that -- it was not that common. You just couldn't get it done.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kind of things did you do for entertainment? Did you have any shows or anything?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: In the Army?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Well, yeah. Down in Panama, I remember one time Bob Hope showed up. But India and China, there was not much. I went to the Taj Mahal up at Agra and we flew up there. Went to the club in Calcutta, which was sort of an isolated American colony. But no, the shows just -- I don't think we ever had one when I was in India and China. Panama, there was two or three of them that showed up. I remember that when Bob Hope came in, we had a huge hangar and that's where he put on his show.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Who else was on the show with Bob, do you remember?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: I really don't remember. I really don't remember [laughter].

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Probably Francis Langford.

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Probably.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any specific memories of mail call, getting letters from home, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Not really. I think that mail was fine in Panama. At the jungle bases it was slow, but it was, you know, pretty consistent. India and China, nobody ever knew where anybody was and stuff could take forever to find you. You know, oh, yeah, he was here last month, yeah. He's been transferred. And so the mail was not -- not real good. I think mailing home was better because, you know, they knew it was going to the United States. And I still have -- my mom and dad saved all my V-mail letters. I have a shopping bag full of letters that are just thrown in there. Someday I should take them out and sort them and see what I told them when I was sitting over there in India.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So anything come to mind as your most vivid memory of that experience?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Not really. I think possibly the first takeoff in the P-40 was very memorable. I mean, it was just something that was a challenge, by us, let's do this, you know. Never knowing what it was, what it was going to be. We had an idea, but we didn't know. But once we got going on those fighter planes, they behaved very comfortable, just like getting in your car and taking off and driving. So those were -- you know, the formation flying and the gunnery and that sort of thing, has good memories. I enjoyed it. I was lucky. I never shot at anybody, and nobody ever shot at me. I think I was in line to, but the war ended, and I was -- I came back whole and everything went fine.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you finally heard they had dropped the bomb, what was your reaction?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Really, it was quiet. We didn't understand. The communications -- to this day I don't know why we didn't know more, but we didn't. It was very, very vague, and the reaction was very quiet. Of course, we were all happy that it was over and we were going to go home, but the communication was really weak. Well, when you're outside of Calcutta 40 or 50 miles, there's, you know, no telephones, and it's -- it's not easy. It was sort of, I'd say, slow and quiet.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing the news that FDR had died?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Don't remember it. I'm sure we heard it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were probably in India at that point? Wasn't it April of '45?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. The communication links were pretty weak in those days. They really were.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have to wait for messages to come to you, then, basically, or how exactly did you get your communication messages, news of any sort without phone lines or that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Well, there were -- there were newspapers or letters, you know, that would be put out by headquarters in Calcutta and distributed, that sort of thing, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You had to wait to read about it.

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Yeah, really. We had a record player. I remember we had one record. We broke all of them but one. We'd sit out on those porches with the thatch-roof huts in India. I guess I remember India more than Panama because it was so different. And we'd listen to records and play Bridge. I played a lot of Bridge. Played chess and pitched horseshoes, because there really wasn't anything to do. We just sat around. That was -- my experience, my wartime experience was not terrifying like a lot of guys went through.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you did your part.

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Well, I did what I had to do.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And, you know, who knows what could have happened if they hadn't dropped the bomb.

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Right. Right. I'm sure we were scheduled to go over. Our squadron was half there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: To be clear, when you talked about that training earlier and the guy was found in the mountains, had he crashed in the mountains?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Yeah, he crashed. Got lost and crashed. And listen, there was a lot of that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I assume he didn't make it, then?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: No. When we graduated and got our wings, the sqaudron commander said, well, now, half of you guys are not coming back. So everybody looked at the guy next to us and said, we'll miss you. And really, it's true. More than half of my roommates got killed. In one -- well, most of -- well, it was accidents, because nobody shot at anybody. Paul Ensminger, my closest buddy, he was killed. He went to China and he was flying C-46s and he -- I heard, I don't know, that his plane crashed into the side of a mountain and killed all the Chinese troops and the Americans on board. And another one I remember that was in Panama in that picture of Howard Field there. You can see where the runways are and where the hangars are. The pilots' ready room was in one of those hangars, the one on the extreme left there, and the runway ended down, it's off the picture, and the guy taking the -- towing the target, when you tow a target for aerial gunnery, the target's strung out behind you, laying on a runway, and the object is to get the airplane off the ground as quick as you can to keep that target from bouncing down the runway, because they had a weight on the bottom of it. Well, this one time, we were all in the pilots' room, and the guy crashed right in front of us. We looked out and here's a P-39 and a big explosion. Because that's a maximum performance maneuver to get that target off, and he's solid, and it Charles W. Olson March 1, 2002 didn't make it. We had breakfast with him, you know [laughter].

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So the target was pulled by a P-39?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Yeah. We towed the target probably 180, 200 miles an hour. Then we had to fly and hit it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't have to do any target towing?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Everybody took their turns.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Bet you took a jaunt (ph) then.

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: So it was --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: [Inaudible].

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: Yeah, it was, it was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any particular, specific memories about your reunion with your girlfriend on New Year's Eve that you can share [laughter]?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: No, it was so great to get home. Went down to the fraternity house, because I was still sort of connected at Case, and I had a lot of goods friends down there, and they had a New Year's Eve party and it was -- it was great to get back.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right. That encompass it?

sp.speaker: Charles Olson
sp.p: That's it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right.
